prompt: One of Edson's developers corrects a pricing program in DEV, and the key users approve it in QAS. What is imported into PRD?
hint: Think about what moved from DEV to QAS.

choices.text: The same transport request that was imported into QAS
choices.why: Right: the request recorded in DEV moves on unchanged, so production gets exactly what was tested.

choices.text: A copy of the QAS program, exported after the test so it carries the fixes found there
choices.why: Nothing is exported from QAS. A fix found in testing goes back to DEV and travels in a new request.

choices.text: The developer repeats the change by hand in PRD
choices.why: PRD is set so that its programs cannot be edited; a change typed again by hand would be untested.

choices.text: A full copy of the DEV system, replacing PRD overnight
choices.why: Each system keeps its own database; copying DEV over PRD would replace production data with development data.

prompt: Put the steps of a change to SAP at Serra Alta in order, from the developer to production.
hint: The figure of the three systems.
items: The change is made in DEV
SAP records it in a transport request
The request is imported into QAS
Key users test it in QAS
The same request is imported into PRD
trap: Importing into PRD before the test in QAS puts untested work into the books.

prompt: The Rota team's test environment connects to QAS, client 300, and posts a batch of test documents. Where do they land?
hint: QAS has two clients, and they are not the same thing.

choices.text: In the testing client, 200, since QAS keeps all test data together
choices.why: Business data is separated by client inside one system; 200 does not see what was posted in 300.

choices.text: Nowhere: SAP refuses a connection that does not name the testing client
choices.why: SAP accepts any client the user is set up in; the connection logs on and posts without complaint.

choices.text: In production, because client numbers are shared across DEV, QAS and PRD
choices.why: Each system has its own database; a client number in QAS reaches nothing in PRD.

choices.text: In the training data that new users learn on
choices.why: Right: client 300 is training, and a connection names a system and a client, so the wrong client gets the documents.

prompt: When the Alagoa plant joins SAP, which kind of change is SAP's own upgrade path designed to carry forward with least effort?
hint: One kind of change is SAP code behaving as configured.

choices.text: A Z report written for the plant
choices.why: A Z object is your code inside SAP; every upgrade has to check it against what changed.

choices.text: A change to SAP's own sales order program, made with a modification key
choices.why: That is a modification of SAP's code, the ring lesson 1 said never to use, and every upgrade has to redo it.

choices.text: Customising: the new plant entered in the Implementation Guide
choices.why: Right: customising is rows in configuration tables that SAP code reads, and SAP designs its upgrades to carry it.

choices.text: A Z table holding the plant’s cheese recipes, read by SAP transactions
choices.why: SAP's upgrade knows nothing of a customer table; it is carried only if somebody checks the code that uses it.

prompt: Marcos asks for UHT litres sold per plant last quarter, from a sales line table with forty fields. Why does a column store answer faster than a row store?
hint: How many of the forty fields does the question need?

choices.text: It reads the three fields it needs and skips the other thirty-seven
choices.why: Right: each column is stored together, so the sum touches three blocks instead of every whole row.

choices.text: It keeps every row of the table in a single block, so one read fetches the whole quarter at once
choices.why: That describes keeping rows together, which is what a row store does and why it has to read all forty fields.

choices.text: It stores pre-computed quarterly totals per plant
choices.why: The opposite: HANA let S/4HANA drop totals tables and compute sums from the line items when asked.

choices.text: It writes nothing to disk, so no read waits for one
choices.why: HANA keeps a log and saves its memory to disk; being in memory is not the reason one column is cheaper than forty.

prompt: A billing line table at Serra Alta has 25 million lines. Its plant column holds one of the three SAP plants, stored as a dictionary and a 2-bit code per line. How many megabytes do the codes take, ignoring the dictionary? (1 MB = 1,000,000 bytes.)
hint: Lines × 2 bits, then 8 bits to a byte.

prompt: If Serra Alta buys every year of extended maintenance SAP offers for ECC 6.0, how many months does it buy after mainstream maintenance ends?
hint: From 1 January 2028 to 31 December 2030.

prompt: Serra Alta converts ECC to S/4HANA in place. Which of these will have to change? Choose all that apply.
hint: Check each one against the table of what S/4HANA removed, and what survives as a view.

choices.text: An EDI map that cuts material numbers at 18 characters
choices.why: Yes: S/4HANA allows 40 characters, and the map breaks on the first longer number.

choices.text: A Z program that writes rows into the index table BSID
choices.why: Yes: BSID survives as a view computed from the line items, and a view is not written to.

choices.text: A Z report whose ABAP reads open customer items from BSID
choices.why: Reads keep working, because the old name answers as a compatibility view.

choices.text: A Z interface that creates customers with no business partner
choices.why: Yes: in S/4HANA every customer and supplier is a business partner.

prompt: A consultant tells Marcos that Serra Alta could simply stay on ECC after 2030 and pay for whatever support SAP still sells. What is the strongest objection for a Brazilian company?
hint: What stops arriving after extended maintenance?

choices.text: Legal changes stop, and the tax reform keeps changing the NF-e until 2033
choices.why: Right: without legal changes the system falls behind the NF-e layout, and without a valid NF-e no pallet ships.

choices.text: ECC stops running on 1 January 2031
choices.why: The software keeps running; what ends is what SAP delivers for it.

choices.text: Its database is no longer supported by any vendor after 2030
choices.why: The lesson gives no such date for the database; the date that matters is SAP’s maintenance for ECC.

choices.text: The 1,800 Z objects stop compiling once mainstream maintenance ends
choices.why: Code keeps compiling on an unchanged system; the Z objects become a problem when the system moves, not when support ends.

prompt: Match each door into SAP to the Serra Alta conversation it suits.
hint: The table "Choosing a door".

pairs.right: a supermarket chain's order arriving through the EDI provider
a bakery waiting on screen for its order number
the portal asking how much butter is available to promise for Friday
a day's milk collection from 1,900 farms, every night

right_distractors: a nightly SQL update of the stock tables

prompt: A supermarket chain says its order reached Serra Alta yesterday: the bus confirms it handed SAP an ORDERS IDoc. SD has no sales order for it. Where does Rui’s team look first?
hint: Accepted and posted are two different moments for an IDoc.

choices.text: In the EDI provider's logs, because a missing order means the IDoc never reached SAP at all
choices.why: The bus confirmed the handover; the IDoc is in SAP, and the question is what happened when it was posted.

choices.text: In the IDoc monitor, for that IDoc stopped in status 51
choices.why: Right: SAP accepted it, then failed to post it, and it waits in status 51 until someone fixes the cause and reprocesses it.

choices.text: In the BAPI return table, which holds the reason the order was refused
choices.why: That table belongs to a synchronous BAPI call; this order came in as an asynchronous IDoc.

choices.text: In the order tables in PRD, with a SQL query by order date
choices.why: If SD has no order, the tables have none either, and the lesson’s rule is not to read them.

prompt: A new integration calls BAPI_SALESORDER_CREATEFROMDAT2, receives an order number and shows it to the user. Next morning SD has no such order. What did the integration most plausibly leave out?
hint: A BAPI that writes needs a second call.

choices.text: An IDoc to confirm the order to SAP afterwards
choices.why: An IDoc is a separate door; the BAPI call is complete in itself once it is committed.

choices.text: A transport request moving the order from DEV into PRD
choices.why: Transports move programs and configuration between systems, never a business document.

choices.text: A check that the returned message table was empty before trusting the number
choices.why: Checking the messages matters, but here a number came back, which means the BAPI did build the order.

choices.text: The call to BAPI_TRANSACTION_COMMIT
choices.why: Right: a BAPI that writes does not commit on its own, so the number belonged to an order that was never saved.

prompt: An IDoc whose application document was posted reaches status 53. One that SAP accepted but could not post stops in status ___ until somebody reprocesses it.
hint: The number Rui’s team watches every morning.

prompt: The Rota team wants farms' bank details for route planning and proposes a read-only database account on SAP: "read-only, so nothing in SAP can break". Which point in the lesson answers that argument most directly?
hint: The argument is about writing. Which problem with reading has nothing to do with writing?

choices.text: A read takes locks that stop clerks working in VA01
choices.why: The lesson’s point about locks concerns writing; it does not say a read blocks clerks.

choices.text: SAP checks authorisations in its application tier, which that login never passes through
choices.why: Right: the login sees every row, including bank data no Rota user is allowed to see through SAP.

choices.text: Reading a table creates documents that count towards the licence
choices.why: The licence register counts documents an integration creates; a read creates none.

choices.text: Read-only accounts stop working during the Sunday maintenance window, and route planning runs on Sundays
choices.why: True of anything synchronous with SAP, and the same for every door; it does not answer the claim that reading is harmless.

prompt: The board pack shows two net sales figures for the same month, and they differ by exactly the month's returns. What is the cause, and who settles it?
hint: Nothing is broken; two definitions are both being applied correctly.

choices.text: Two universes define the measure differently; Marcos decides which is right
choices.why: Right: the definition lives in the semantic layer, and which one is correct is a finance decision, not a tool setting.

choices.text: A bug in Web Intelligence, fixed by the BusinessObjects team with the next upgrade
choices.why: Both reports compute exactly what their universe says; an upgrade would reproduce both numbers.

choices.text: BW loaded the returns late, so one report ran before the nightly extraction
choices.why: A timing gap would differ from day to day; a gap exactly equal to the returns every month points at the definition.

choices.text: One report reads production and the other reads BW
choices.why: At Serra Alta the universes query BW; the lesson traces the two figures to two definitions of the measure.

prompt: A bakery moved from the Juiz de Fora sales region to Barbacena's in June. Why does BW still credit its January sales to Juiz de Fora when a report run against SAP would not?
hint: What does SAP do to a master record when it changes?

choices.text: SAP keeps every past version of the customer record
choices.why: SAP overwrites the master record; the old region is gone from it.

choices.text: BW is refreshed once a year, so it has not heard about the move yet, and catches up at year end
choices.why: Extractors send changes every night; BW knows about the move and still keeps the old region on the old sales.

choices.text: BW kept the region each sale had when it happened
choices.why: Right: the warehouse remembers what the ERP overwrites, which is what the regional bonuses are calculated on.

choices.text: The universe hard-codes the region on each bakery
choices.why: A universe maps names onto tables and calculations; history comes from how BW stored the facts.

prompt: Twelve months of audit show 300 of the 900 reports unopened. Joana wants them gone before the S/4HANA project starts. What is the right next step?
hint: Some reports are opened once a year.

choices.text: Delete the 300 now, since twelve months without a reader is proof enough
choices.why: An annual report, such as the FSSC 22000 batch records, falls outside a twelve-month window by a few weeks.

choices.text: Migrate all 900 to S/4HANA and clean up afterwards, so that no user loses a report
choices.why: Carrying the 300 means paying to convert and test them, and cleaning up is cheaper before the move than during it.

choices.text: Rebuild the 300 in SAP Analytics Cloud
choices.why: Rebuilding a report nobody reads moves the cost to a new product instead of removing it.

choices.text: Measure over more than a year, find each owner, and archive rather than delete
choices.why: Right: a longer window catches the annual reports, and an archive comes back if somebody asks.

prompt: After a move to S/4HANA, which argument against reporting straight on production still stands?
hint: One argument was about load on a row database.

choices.text: A long scan of order lines slows down the clerks taking orders
choices.why: This is the argument HANA weakens: a column store answers many such questions on live data without hurting transactions.

choices.text: Reports on production cannot use universes
choices.why: The lesson makes no such claim; the argument is about what production holds, not which tool reads it.

choices.text: Production holds one system’s current state, not history or other systems
choices.why: Right: the bakery’s old region and the cheese plant’s sales in Business Central are not in S/4HANA.

choices.text: Live figures change during the day, and the board prefers figures fixed at midnight by the nightly load
choices.why: Freshness is what reporting on production gains; the lesson’s remaining argument is about history and breadth.

prompt: Talita wants a rep's order to reach SAP while the rep waits, and to show the SAP order number at once. Which belong in Joana's design? Choose all that apply.
hint: The door, its two habits, the register, and where tests point.

choices.text: A BAPI called over RFC through the bus, followed by the commit
choices.why: Yes: a rep waiting for a number needs a synchronous call, and a BAPI that writes needs the commit.

choices.text: Testing against PRD, client 100, because QAS data is less realistic
choices.why: Tests point at QAS and never at PRD; keeping QAS realistic is the work to do instead.

choices.text: Reading the returned messages, not only the order number
choices.why: Yes: a BAPI reports failure as data, and a caller reading only the number reads an empty one as success.

choices.text: A line in the register: about how many sales orders a month it creates
choices.why: Yes: the documents an integration creates are what indirect use is priced on, so the contracts team needs the count.

prompt: Sebastião asks whether Coleta’s nightly file must change for a brownfield move to S/4HANA. What should Joana tell him?
hint: The file is one thing; the Z program that reads it is another.

choices.text: Yes: goods receipts move to MATDOC, so Coleta has to write a new layout
choices.why: MATDOC is inside SAP; Coleta never sees a table, so the file layout is not what the new table changes.

choices.text: No: a brownfield conversion keeps everything, so nothing on either side of the file changes
choices.why: It keeps the Z program, but every Z object is checked against the Simplification List, the loader included.

choices.text: The file is unaffected; the Z loader is checked, and posting through SAP's logic decides the work
choices.why: Right: if the loader posts goods receipts through SAP’s own logic it carries over easily; if it writes tables itself, it is rewritten.

choices.text: Only if the loader appears in the usage log as unused
choices.why: The loader runs every night at 02:00, so it is the opposite of a deletion candidate.

prompt: On the third working day of the month, Rui's team finds that a change inside SAP is needed to stop EDI orders failing. What happens to it?
hint: Two calendars meet here: the transport windows and the close.

choices.text: It goes into PRD that evening, because EDI failures cost sales
choices.why: Imports stop in the first five working days while finance closes; urgency alone does not reopen the window.

choices.text: Rui’s team edits the mapping in PRD directly and records it in DEV afterwards
choices.why: PRD cannot be edited, and the auditors who certify the books check that setting.

choices.text: It skips QAS so that it reaches the Tuesday import
choices.why: A request reaches PRD after QAS, in release order; skipping the test does not move the calendar.

choices.text: It waits for the window after the close, unless Edson signs an emergency transport
choices.why: Right: the close week freezes imports, and an emergency transport is the one exception, decided by Edson.
